*Lecture 20 · Fri Oct 16, 2026 · notes + slides "Discrete Fourier transform" · prev: [[4-sampling-and-reconstruction/19-aliasing|Lecture 19]] · next: [[5-dft-and-fft/21-dft-properties|Lecture 21]]*

> [!abstract] In one breath
> - A computer cannot evaluate the DTFT: the sum is infinite and $\omega$ is continuous.
> - The DFT keeps $N$ samples and $N$ frequencies: $X[k]=X_d\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{N}\right)$, $0\le k\le N-1$.
> - $X[k]$ and the inverse DFT are $N$-periodic; zero padding samples the same $X_d(\omega)$ more densely.

## 1. Computing the DTFT

Writing a function that returns (notes eq. 1, slides 3–5)

$$
X_d(\omega)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}
$$

runs into two problems.

**(1) The sum is infinite.** Keep $0\le n\le N-1$ (eqs. 2–4):

$$
\hat X_d(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]w[n]e^{-j\omega n},\qquad w[n]=\begin{cases}1, & 0\le n\le N-1\\ 0, & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$

- This **windows** $x[n]$. By the windowing property (eq. 5), $x[n]w[n]\overset{\mathcal F}{\longleftrightarrow}\frac{1}{2\pi}X_d(\omega)*W_d(\omega)$ (periodic convolution), so $\hat X_d(\omega)\ne X_d(\omega)$.
- Window functions: upcoming lectures.

**(2) $\omega$ is continuous.** Even a length-$N$ signal has $X_d(\omega)$ at infinitely many $\omega$. $X_d$ is $2\pi$-periodic, so sample one period at $N$ regularly spaced frequencies (eq. 6):

$$
\omega_k=\frac{2\pi k}{N},\qquad0\le k\le N-1 .
$$

Both fixes together (eq. 7):

$$
\hat X_k=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n}.
$$

- Almost the [[concepts/fourier-series|DTFS]] analysis equation, with $N$ for $N_0$: $x[n]$ is not assumed periodic, only of length $N$ (by windowing or by nature).
- More than $N$ frequencies are possible: §2.3.

## 2. Discrete Fourier transform

> [!key] DFT (notes eqs. 8–9, slide 6)
> For a length-$N$ signal $x[n]$, $x[n]\overset{\text{DFT}}{\longleftrightarrow}X[k]$:
> $$
> X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n},\qquad0\le k\le N-1\qquad\text{(analysis, forward DFT)}
> $$
> $$
> x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n},\qquad0\le n\le N-1\qquad\text{(synthesis, inverse DFT)}
> $$
> $X[k]$ is defined for $0\le k\le N-1$ only.

### 2.1 Relationship between DTFT and DFT

For a length-$N$ $x[n]$, $X_d(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}$ (eq. 10). The DFT is the same sum at $\omega=\omega_k$ (eq. 11).

> [!key] The DFT samples the DTFT (eq. 12)
> $$
> X[k]=X_d(\omega)\Big|_{\omega=\omega_k}=X_d\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{N}\right),\qquad0\le k\le N-1 .
> $$
> $N$ regularly spaced samples from $\omega=0$ up to, not including, $2\pi$; spacing $\frac{2\pi}{N}$.

n ≤ 4 and 1 for 5 ≤ n ≤ 9; the 10-point DFT (orange) takes |X<sub>d</sub>(ω)| (solid) at ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/10: X[0] = 15, and X[k] = 0 for even k ≠ 0.</figcaption></figure>

- $X_d$ is $2\pi$-periodic, so a bin with $k\gt\frac N2$ is the negative frequency $\omega_k-2\pi$. For $N=10$: $X[9]=X_d\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{5}\right)$.

### 2.2 N-periodicity of the DFT

> [!key] $N$-periodicity (eqs. 13–19, slides 9–10)
> $$
> X[k]=X[k+mN],\qquad m\in\mathbb Z .
> $$
> The inverse DFT is $N$-periodic too: $\bar x[n]=\mathrm{IDFT}\{X[k]\}$ satisfies $\bar x[n+mN]=\bar x[n]$. The DFT implies the **periodic extension** of the length-$N$ signal.

> [!derivation]- Proofs (slides 9–10)
> $e^{-j2\pi mn}=e^{j2\pi km}=1$ for integers $k$, $m$, $n$:
> $$
> X[k+mN]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n}e^{-j2\pi mn}=X[k],
> $$
> $$
> \bar x[n+mN]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n}e^{j2\pi km}=\bar x[n].
> $$
> Slide 10's "$x[n]=x[k+mN]$" means $x[n]=x[n+mN]$.

The notes return to periodic extension next lecture: [[5-dft-and-fft/21-dft-properties|Lecture 21]] (circular shifts, circular convolution).

### 2.3 Zero-padding

> [!key] Zero padding (eqs. 20–25)
> Append $L$ zeros:
> $$
> \tilde x[n]=\begin{cases}x[n], & 0\le n\le N-1\\ 0, & N\le n\le N+L-1\end{cases}
> $$
> Same nonzero samples, so the same DTFT, $\tilde X_d(\omega)=X_d(\omega)$, and
> $$
> \tilde X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi k}{N+L}n}=X_d\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{N+L}\right),\qquad0\le k\le N+L-1 .
> $$
> Spacing $\frac{2\pi}{N+L}$ instead of $\frac{2\pi}{N}$: a denser view of the same spectrum, for the cost of a longer DFT.

> [!recipe] Which padded bin equals $X[k]$?
> Equate frequencies, $\frac{2\pi k}{N}=\frac{2\pi k'}{N+L}$: $k'=\frac{(N+L)\,k}{N}$, a match only when it is an integer.

> [!question] Notes Exercise 1
> $x[n]$ has length 16 and DFT $X[k]$. Zero-pad it with 48 zeros to the length-64 $\tilde x[n]$ with DFT $\tilde X[k]$. Which values of $\tilde X[k]$ equal (a) $X[1]$, (b) $X[9]$?

> [!success]- Answer (eqs. 26–31)
> (a) $X[1]$ sits at $\frac{2\pi\cdot1}{16}=\frac{\pi}{8}$; $\frac{2\pi k}{64}=\frac{\pi}{8}\Rightarrow k=4$: $\boldsymbol{X[1]=\tilde X[4]}$.
>
> (b) $\frac{2\pi k}{64}=\frac{2\pi\cdot9}{16}\Rightarrow k=36$: $\boldsymbol{X[9]=\tilde X[36]}$.

> [!question] Slides — Zero-padding Example 1
> $x[n]$ has length 16 and DFT $X[k]$. Zero-pad it with 32 zeros to $y[n]$ with DFT $Y[k]$. Which values of $Y[k]$ equal (a) $X[0]$, (b) $X[1]$, (c) $X[4]$?

> [!success]- Answer
> Length $48=3\cdot16$, so $\frac{2\pi k}{16}=\frac{2\pi\cdot3k}{48}$: $\boldsymbol{X[0]=Y[0]}$, $\boldsymbol{X[1]=Y[3]}$, $\boldsymbol{X[4]=Y[12]}$.

> [!question] Slides — Zero-padding Example 2
> A length-$N$ signal $x[n]\overset{\mathcal F}{\longleftrightarrow}X_d(\omega)$. We want the DFT $X[k]$ to contain $X_d\!\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right)$ and $X_d\!\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$. What are the two smallest possible values of $N$?

> [!success]- Answer
> Need integers $k_1$, $k_2$ with $\frac{2\pi k_1}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5}$ and $\frac{2\pi k_2}{N}=\frac{\pi}{3}$: $N=10k_1=6k_2$, a multiple of $\mathrm{lcm}(10,6)=30$. Two smallest: $\boldsymbol{N=30}$ ($k_1=3$, $k_2=5$) and $\boldsymbol{N=60}$ ($k_1=6$, $k_2=10$). Zero-pad $x[n]$ to reach them.

### 2.4 Linear algebra formulation (optional)

- Each $X[k]$ is a dot product (eqs. 32–34): $X[k]=\mathbf v^*\mathbf u$ with $\mathbf u=x[n]$, $\mathbf v=e^{j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n}$, $n=0,\dots,N-1$; $\mathbf v^*$ is the conjugate transpose.
- Example $N=5$, $k=3$ (eq. 35):

$$
X[3]=\begin{bmatrix}1 & e^{-j\frac{2\pi\cdot3}{5}\cdot1} & e^{-j\frac{2\pi\cdot3}{5}\cdot2} & e^{-j\frac{2\pi\cdot3}{5}\cdot3} & e^{-j\frac{2\pi\cdot3}{5}\cdot4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x[0]\\ x[1]\\ x[2]\\ x[3]\\ x[4]\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Twiddle factor $W_N=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}}$, so $W_N^{kn}=e^{-j\frac{2\pi k}{N}n}$ (eqs. 37–38; eq. 36's $W=e^{-j2\pi}$ is missing the $N$).

> [!key] DFT matrix (eqs. 39–45)
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> \mathbf X=\mathbf W\mathbf x,\qquad\mathbf W=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\\ 1 & W_N & W_N^2 & \cdots & W_N^{N-1}\\ 1 & W_N^2 & W_N^4 & \cdots & W_N^{2(N-1)}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 1 & W_N^{N-1} & W_N^{2(N-1)} & \cdots & W_N^{(N-1)(N-1)}\end{bmatrix},\\
> \mathbf W_{kn}=W_N^{kn}.
> \end{gathered}
> $$
> Row $k$ is the complex exponential $e^{-j\omega_kn}$, $\omega_k=\frac{2\pi k}{N}$. Inverse: $\mathbf x=\mathbf W^{-1}\mathbf X$, $\mathbf W^{-1}=\frac1N\mathbf W^*$ (conjugate transpose).

- Why it matters: each $X[k]$ is visibly the dot product of $x[n]$ with one exponential; $\mathbf W$ and $\mathbf W^{-1}$ can be precomputed, and optimized matrix–vector products beat a double for-loop.

> [!question] Lecture exercise
> Discuss how the columns of $\mathbf W$ form an orthogonal set of basis vectors for $\mathbb C^N$.

> [!success]- Answer
> Inner product of columns $n$ and $n'$: $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(W_N^{kn'}\right)^*W_N^{kn}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}k(n-n')}$.
> - $n=n'$: $N$.
> - $n\ne n'$: geometric series with ratio $r=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}(n-n')}\ne1$ and $r^N=1$, so $\frac{1-r^N}{1-r}=0$.
>
> So $\mathbf W^*\mathbf W=N\mathbf I$: $N$ orthogonal nonzero vectors in $\mathbb C^N$, a basis. The same identity gives $\mathbf W^{-1}=\frac1N\mathbf W^*$.

> [!trap] Where points go
> - **Bins past $\frac N2$ are negative frequencies:** $X[k]=X_d\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{N}-2\pi\right)$.
> - **Zero padding never changes $X_d(\omega)$;** it only refines the DFT grid.
> - **Padded bin $\frac{(N+L)k}{N}$, not $k$:** in general $X[1]\ne\tilde X[1]$.
> - **The inverse DFT is $N$-periodic,** not zero outside $0\le n\le N-1$: the inverse DFT of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ has $x[4]=x[0]=2.5$.
> - **$\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2\pi}{6}$ needs $N$ a multiple of 6,** not 3: $N=15$ gives $k=2.5$.
